items.title: NAR sees pent-up demand waiting on lower mortgage rates, better sentiment
items.description: The U.S. housing market is building “significant” pent-up demand that could be released if mortgage rates ease, inventory improves and consumer confidence rebounds, National Association of Realtors’ (NAR) chief economist Lawrence Yun told attendees Friday at NAR’s NXT in New Orleans. Yun contrasted today’s sales environmen t with the year 2000, noting that the U.S. population has grown from 281 million to 350 million and payroll jobs from 132 million to 159 million over that period. Housing wealth has ballooned from $7 trillion to $35 trillion, yet existing-home sales are tracking near 4 million this year , well below the 5.2 million homes sold in 2000, he said, citing NAR data. “Affordability is tough, but people’s incomes are rising, and if somehow mortgage rates go down, think about the potential housing demand that could be released to the marketplace,” Yun said. On the supply side, Yun said inventory has risen as sales have slowed. Months’ supply is now at its highest level since 2015, and the median home took 33 days to go from listing to contract in September, according to NAR. “Homes are staying on the market a little longer than before,” Yun said. “With longer days on market, you have to be realistic to the market condition. Otherwise, buyers will reject the homes on the market.” Yun pointed to consumer psychology as a key missing ingredient. Consumer sentiment has fallen to roughly half its 2000 level and is now worse than during the Great Recession, even as the labor market has added jobs. “If we can boost confidence levels, maybe that can also change the dynamics,” Yun said. First-time buyers remain near historic lows Jessica Lautz, NAR deputy chief economist and vice president of research, presented findings from the trade group’s newly released 2026 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers . First-time buyers made up 22% of all buyers, near the series low, and the median age of first-time buyers held at a record-high 40. Those numbers underscore how younger households are delaying homeownership, even as they form households and enter peak earning years. For lenders and real estate brokerages, that means fewer entry-level transactions and more emphasis on move-up or equity-rich buyers. “ First-time home buyers are struggling,” Lautz said. “They’re not struggling just with housing affordability. They're also struggling with rent. They’re struggling with student loan debt, and a rising issue for first-time home buyers is childcare costs.” Lautz noted that sellers reported staying in their homes for a median of 12 years before selling, the longest tenure on record for the survey. “The golden handcuffs of low interest rate mortgages is true. People are holding on to those properties for longer periods of time,” she said. “It’s why we need to build more housing inventory—especially affordable housing inventory—for the potential first-time home buyers who are out there.” Agent usage hits record highs Despite technology and direct-to-consumer platforms, use of licensed professionals in transactions remained strong, according to NAR’s survey. A reported 90% of buyers purchased through an agent, the highest share in four decades, and a record 92% of sellers used an agent. “Sellers want agents to price that home competitively, find that qualified buyer, help with marketing, and make sure they get to the closing table in a time frame that they need to do so,” Lautz said. Why this matters for housing professionals For real estate agents and brokers, NAR’s data point to a market where transaction volume is constrained more by affordability, rates and sentiment than by underlying demand. A larger population, more jobs and higher housing wealth suggest that activity could accelerate quickly if mortgage rates retreat and confidence improves. For lenders, a 22% first-time buyer share and a median first-time buyer age of 40 highlight both near-term headwinds and an eventual backlog of delayed demand. Households that are renting longer and juggling student debt and childcare may respond strongly to any easing in rates, pricing or down payment constraints. For builders and developers, Lautz’s comments reinforce the policy and business case for adding affordable inventory . With existing owners locked in by sub-4% mortgages and staying put for a median 12 years, new construction remains one of the few levers to ease the entry-level shortage. Yun’s and Lautz’s remarks come as the industry also adjusts to p ost-settlement commission rule changes and elevated borrowing costs , making accurate pricing, counseling on affordability and clear communication with consumers more central to winning business in 2027 and beyond. items.title: What NAR's new MLS policy options mean for data feeds and licensing
items.description: The National Association of Realtors (NAR) has approved four multiple listing service (MLS) policy recommendations that increase MLSs’ options to claim copyright in listing content, expand local flexibility on data feeds, clarify permissible uses of MLS data and update qualifications for NAR’s MLS Committee. The recommendations from NAR’s Multiple Listing Issues and Policies Committee were considered and adopted at NAR NXT 2026 conference on Sunday and are tied to the trade group’s 2026-2028 strategic plan to modernize MLS policies, the association said in an announcement Sunday. New optional copyright policy for MLS data The most consequential change for brokers and MLS operators is a revision to MLS Policy Statement 7.85 and the creation of a new optional policy on copyright protection of MLS data. Under the revised policy, MLSs may, at their discretion, require up to a 50% copyright interest in certain listing content to strengthen copyright enforcement, subject to quarterly copyright registration requirements. MLSs must give participants the right to opt out of assigning a copyright interest to the MLS, and brokers retain the right to independently use and license their own listing content. Copyright ownership and enforcement have become more important as listing photos and data are syndicated across portals, IDX sites and marketing platforms, and as MLSs face more frequent questions and disputes about unauthorized scraping and reuse of listing content. Greater local flexibility on data feeds NAR also adopted an optional MLS policy on MLS data feed services. The policy allows MLSs to establish local eligibility and licensing requirements for data feeds, as long as those rules are reasonable, objective and applied equally to all participants. Even with new local rules, participants must retain access to MLS listing information and data feeds for their own listings. For brokers and vendors, this could affect how quickly and under what conditions they can obtain broader data feeds for tools such as brokerage websites, back-office systems and analytics products, depending on how individual MLSs choose to implement the optional policy. Clarification on permitted MLS data uses A new MLS policy statement reinforces that the use of MLS data must comply with applicable MLS participation or data licensing agreements and must be connected to real estate brokerage services, the preparation of appraisals or other valuations of real property. NAR said this is intended to address concerns around unauthorized use of MLS content, including use cases that are not connected to providing brokerage or valuation services. For MLSs, this language provides additional backing for enforcement actions against parties that use listing data for unrelated commercial purposes. For brokers and appraisers, it underscores the need to align technology partnerships and data workflows with the scope of their MLS agreements. Updated qualifications for NAR’s MLS Committee NAR also updated the qualification criteria for service on its MLS Committee. The changes are meant to better reflect today’s MLS environment and ensure the committee includes members with relevant industry expertise and perspectives. While specific qualification details were not outlined in the announcement, changes to committee composition can influence how future policy recommendations are shaped and how regional and business-model interests are represented at the national level. “These updates reflect our commitment to ensuring MLS policies remain relevant, effective, and responsive to the needs of today’s real estate industry,” Nykia Wright, the CEO of NAR and a 2026 HousingWire Woman of Influence and Vanguard award winner, said in the announcement. “In line with our 2026–2028 Strategic Plan and significant member feedback, we will continue working collaboratively with MLSs, brokers, members, and other industry partners to support a clear understanding and implementation of these changes.” Next steps for MLSs and brokers Because several of the policies are optional , local MLSs will have to decide whether and how to adopt them. MLS executives and boards will likely review their copyright strategies, data feed agreements and committee engagement structures in light of the new framework. Brokers, teams and technology vendors should review their MLS participation and data licensing agreements to understand how any local policy changes could affect website data feeds, marketing uses of listing content and third-party integrations. items.title: 'Certainty Will Be The Buzzword': Stability, Not Sea Change, For CRE Post-Midterm
items.description: The implications of an overwhelming Democratic midterm victory reverberated through markets in the second half of last week, reflecting skittishness among investors and business leaders over fears about the impact on the largest driver of today's economy: data center growth. Despite these initial shocks, there is a quiet expectation that a Democratic Congress will help bring calm to a period of significant economic volatility stemming in part from the unpredictable policymaking that has emerged during President Donald Trump 's second term. “Maybe ‘uncertainty’ was the buzzword of the last year, and hopefully ‘certainty’ will be the buzzword going forward,” said Jeff DeBoer , CEO of the Washington, D.C.-based trade group The Real Estate Roundtable . “We're much more certain that we're not going to wake up every day and have another wild fluctuation in some sort of policy.” Unsplash/Sebastian Schuster That semblance of certainty won't be a panacea, however. Major relief from the ubiquitous issues for commercial real estate today, including higher costs, low labor availability and expensive debt, is unlikely to come from the new Congress because those issues are closely tied to Trump's executive actions and powers. But housing affordability, the economy more generally and data centers were on the ballot in races around the country, where the results have set the stage for a string of policy debates that will hit landlords and investors. “If you look back in history, there are a number of examples where a great amount of very positive legislation has been done when there's divided government,” DeBoer said. “I'm not one who says, ‘Put your feet up, nothing's going to happen, we're in for gridlock.’ I think there's going to be some significant legislation.” Stock traders initially reacted positively to the midterm results, with all three major indexes climbing, but the mood changed Thursday. A massive sell-off focused on tech stocks but spread marketwide sucked $2.5T in market value out of the Nasdaq and pushed the index into correction territory. By Friday, the dust had settled and markets opened by gaining back some of Thursday’s losses. Investors are trying to reprice their bets on the pace of the artificial intelligence infrastructure build-out as they weigh the prospect of a Congress that is more skeptical of the major tech firms’ plans and a wave of local fervor against data centers that drove voters to the polls. AI and data centers emerged as a key political flashpoint, with more than half of respondents telling an NBC exit poll that it was a crucial or major factor in their decision to vote in the midterms. Across statewide races and referendums, voters roundly supported measures putting limits on data center development in more than 40 local ballot measures . “This election, whether federally or on the local level, was influenced by data centers,” said Commercial Real Estate Development Association CEO Marc Selvitelli. “This was the rare bipartisan issue that was out there right now.” The economy emerged as the top issue for voters headed into the election after the U.S. war with Iran drove up energy costs and added to already elevated inflation. The president’s tariffs are also contributing to the rising costs, but the Democratic sweep in Congress still has limited reach into trade policy that’s coming directly from the White House. "The swing in Congress, the results of the election, are very unlikely to have a significant impact on the president's trade agenda and the tariffs that are in place," Blake Harden, managing director for trade policy at ​ Ernst & Young 's Washington Council office, told Reuters . "This is because there is so much trade authority within the executive branch that's been delegated by Congress." Unsplash/Jesse Paul Democrats have floated the idea of changing the tariff laws the president is relying on to impose his protectionist trade regime, but the party would need to win over some Republicans because it remains short of a veto-proof majority. They’re also working on a plan to roll back Trump’s tariffs directed at Canada, The Wall Street Journal reported Thursday. “The midterm election results are unlikely to materially influence commercial real estate performance,” Cushman & Wakefield analysts wrote in a postelection report . A divided government adds some degree of fiscal policy stability that “should be calming for markets,” although the U.S. war in Iran and the downstream impacts on prices and inflation remain the greatest “swing factor for inflation and rates,” they wrote. The election was at least in part a referendum on the war in Iran, according to Hans Nordby , executive managing director of research and investment analytics at Transwestern . “And it was a ‘no’ vote,” Nordby wrote in an email to Bisnow on Friday. “The new Congress could defund the war or otherwise force a withdrawal. If that were to happen, it would seem likely that oil prices could retreat to prewar levels, which would put downward pressure on inflation.” The war and its economic fallout, particularly on the price of oil, has been a thorn in CRE's side since it broke out in February. The rising cost of oil has contributed to overall inflation remaining elevated, which in turn has kept borrowing rates higher. Yields for 10-year U.S. Treasury bonds , a key benchmark rate for all sorts of debt costs, notched lower following the midterms after climbing above 5% in October before retreating, shedding 6 basis points Wednesday and continuing to trade below 4.9% through Friday. items.title: Can the new Congress help lower mortgage rates?
items.description: After the Democrats' historic midterm win , the question now is: can the new Congress help get mortgage rates lower? Obviously, the Iran conflict and trade war have taken their toll on President Trump's approval ratings, but can Congress — both Democrats and Republicans — now work together on getting something done that the President will not veto? Let's look at the economic factors influencing rates in this environment, what Congress can do about each, and how the Fed might consider these as they set monetary policy. 1. Oil and diesel prices When WTI oil was at $112 on April 7 this year, the 10-year yield was at 4.31% — but back then the Fed was still talking about cutting rates two to three times. A lot has changed since then. The Federal Reserve has made the Iran conflict a big talking point, so some type of resolution to this conflict could impact rates. Obviously, the conflict has hurt President Trump and the Republicans; it’s very unpopular, especially with farmers and truckers who have to deal with high diesel prices. Trump himself acknowledged the war played a major part in the midterm results. Congress made some attempts to try to end this conflict in the past, but may have renewed incentives now to find a solution. We shall see what comes next, as President Trump has said he could make a deal after the midterms. 2. The AI boom Now, the AI boom is a little bit more complicated because there are a lot of projects still in the pipeline that can’t be shut down by the Democrats right now, but future projects could definitely be affected. And with some type of regulation and moratorium, some of the growth prospects might be slowed down. This is a critical factor because the Federal Reserve has really made the AI boom and inflation a hot topic. It’s part of the reason why, when you see AI softness — whether it’s the credit markets or their stock prices getting hit — bond traders tend to want to buy bonds, not sell them, in that environment. For now, the Fed needs to see a material slowdown to lose its hawkish stance on AI, but it would be another positive for rates. On another note, the labor productivity data was awesome today. This data really affects how the Fed sees AI and will be the best news for mortgage rates if this trend continues. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh himself has made a dovish case around AI as long as it creates more productivity and lowers labor unit costs. Here is the chart of the 10-year yield for the last six months as of this second, the 10-year yield is down once again to 4.83% as AI stocks are selling off. 3. Trade war 2.0 This will be very interesting because I am sure President Trump will try every legal angle to continue his tariff policy — he still wants to have tariffs because it’s his favorite tool to cut deals. However, what the midterms have done is limit the power he can have to escalate the trade war into something worse. That can be a very big positive: we might have seen the high of the 10-year yield at 5.35% if the trade war doesn’t get worse amid the conflict with Iran. For now, we need to wait and see how much farther the President wants to push the trade war. He might just cut a deal with Canada, leave other countries alone and just focus on China — which would be a positive for rates. 4. Jobs Usually, in an economic cycle, when manufacturing jobs and construction jobs are being lost, it’s not a good sign for the labor market: we saw that in 2025. But the labor market has improved this year and that has kept the Fed's focus fully on inflation. One thing to think about going forward is that, if we do have some data center moratoriums and rates stay elevated, construction labor might get hit a little bit harder than before the midterms. If the unemployment rate rises as growth slows down, that will be a positive for mortgage rates. Conclusion For rates to really make a meaningful move lower and stick, three of the four things above need to get better. You need to get oil prices trading between $67 and $82. You need to get diesel prices down so the Fed won’t talk about energy prices being passed onto the consumer. You've got to de-escalate the trade war 2.0 and get some deals in and not make it inflationary. The AI moratorium and regulations will be a welcome signal to the Federal Reserve; whether that impacts the construction data enough to matter to them is still an open question, but the three things above need to occur to have rates go under 7% and stay there. items.title: Trump strikes a softer note on immigration; builders need proof
items.description: On Sunday, President Donald Trump indicated that he is open to negotiating an immigration deal with the incoming Democratic Congress. However, despite softening post-election rhetoric, the Trump administration appears to be sending mixed signals on immigration, clouding the outlook for any potential bipartisan agreement. The stakes of the nation’s highly contentious immigration debate remain high for homebuilders. After a surge in job site raids by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) this summer and fall, many homebuilders say their workers, including those in the country legally, were swept up in enforcement actions . Whether a bipartisan immigration deal materializes remains an open and pressing question for the numerous builders facing ongoing job site disruptions. Speaking to CBS News’ 60 Minutes on Sunday, President Trump suggested his administration’s immigration policies “might be too tough” and may have contributed to last week’s election outcome. “When you go into a hotel…and you have a woman that's worked there as a maid, as a cleaner, as a this, as a that, as a waitress – a lot of good things, great jobs – and all of a sudden, they're being taken out of the country. It's tough. It's a tough thing,” Trump said. Trump added that it may be “doable” to reach an agreement allowing undocumented workers who have lived in the U.S. for many years, construction workers among them, to legally remain in the country. “Get the killers out. Get the rapists out. Get all the rough ones out. Get the drug dealers out, but let the people that are here, and in some cases here for 10 and 15 years, work a deal for them,” Trump suggested. The administration’s mixed messaging It’s unclear whether Trump’s softer rhetoric will translate into a bipartisan immigration deal. However, his administration’s decision to promote Stephen Miller, a longtime immigration hardliner, to White House Chief of Staff suggests an agreement may be less likely than Trump implied in his CBS News interview. And in a post on Sunday, the Official White House Rapid Response account, in a post on X , denied that Trump will push for an amnesty deal with Democrats. However, Trump has at times shown a willingness to soften his stance on immigration, at least briefly. In June 2025, the Trump administration momentarily directed ICE to pause job site raids in sectors like agriculture, hospitality and restaurants after facing blowback from business leaders worried about staffing shortages. Within days, however, the administration reversed course. It later set a target of 3,000 ICE arrests per day, leading to a record number of immigration arrests in recent months. Trump has also helped kill a bipartisan deal before. In early 2024, ahead of the presidential election, he urged Republicans to vote against a Senate border package introduced by Sen. James Lankford (R-OK) that would have tightened asylum requirements, ended releases of migrants into U.S. communities while they await hearings, and let the president close the border when asylum claims surged. The bill ultimately failed. Some homebuilding organizations, like the National Association of Home Builders, now have their eyes on a different bipartisan measure, the Dignity Act , which would allow certain undocumented workers to remain in the U.S. without citizenship. Trump’s words signaled openness to such a proposal, but the administration’s actions since the election suggest otherwise. Vice President JD Vance, meanwhile, laid out in a post-midterms election post on X that the administration may be open to changing its approach to immigration, with less room for negotiation. “Expect to hear any number of establishment politicians say the solution to our woes is amnesty. I'm open to the idea that we should change enforcement – by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance. But anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you,” Vance wrote. For homebuilders, immigration policy and its impact on the construction labor pool remains among the biggest policy questions heading into 2027. However, history suggests that a bipartisan deal may be a heavy lift, as Washington hasn’t passed comprehensive immigration reform since 1986, under President Reagan. Whether Washington breaks its four-decade drought on immigration reform, and whether enforcement eases on job sites, remains a key policy wild card to watch in 2027. items.title: What View Homes' rebrand says about Gandhi’s operating overhaul
items.description: Seven months into her effort to transform View Homes from a loose collection of regional builders into a cohesive enterprise, CEO Natasha Gandhi has drawn a line between the company's past and its ambitions. A newly unified brand makes that promise visible. Now Gandhi and her team must overdeliver on it. View Homes announced Monday a new corporate brand identity, unifying its formerly distinct Aspen View, Desert View, Horizon View and View Homes operations under one name. The change spans five divisions across Colorado, New Mexico and Texas and marks a milestone in the operational transformation Gandhi began after becoming CEO in March 2026. The announcement also comes one week after View's parent, Hunt Companies , joined with global investment manager Wafra to launch Strata Land Partners , a new land-financing platform led by former Landsea Homes president Michael Forsum. Together, these developments offer a clearer view of Hunt's expanding ambitions in U.S. residential construction and development. In an exclusive interview with HousingWire TBD , Gandhi said the branding initiative is part of a broader effort to prepare View for growth, strengthen operating standards, and compete across more markets and homebuyer segments. "We want to be a premium builder, and by premium, it's not that we're unaffordable," Gandhi said. "It just means that we want to be the best in every price point that we're out there, we want to be the best in every market that we build in." One brand, one operating standard Hunt acquired full ownership of View Homes in 2025, inheriting an established 35-year-old homebuilding business whose regional operations had developed distinct identities, systems and operating practices. When Gandhi arrived in March, she found an organization with strong local relationships and experienced teams, but lacking the consistent management processes, reporting systems, and enterprise infrastructure needed to support the growth Hunt envisioned. As The Builder's Daily reported in October , Gandhi's initial work focused on leadership changes, clearer accountability, more disciplined sales concessions, selective land investment, and a comprehensive review of enterprise technology. The new branding establishes four standards intended to apply across the organization: exceptional customer experience, people-first leadership, design-forward homes, and premium quality across price points. "I felt like previously, we had different standards in different markets, but now with this new brand, it really sets the stage," Gandhi said. "These four pillars are something that is now going to be operationally executed in all our markets." The challenge is to translate those commitments into consistent performance without compromising the local knowledge and customer relationships that have made View's regional businesses successful. For a multiregional homebuilder, Gandhi notes, that means more than consistent signage and marketing. It requires shared expectations for product quality, customer service, sales execution, and management accountability, supported by reliable information and operating systems. The work behind the promise Gandhi is candid that the transformation remains unfinished. "This is just the start of our growth journey," she said. "I will tell you, we're not there yet, but we're on the path of getting there." The branding initiative has prompted further scrutiny of the operational capabilities needed to support the company's ambitions to up its game. Gandhi acknowledged that View's enterprise resource planning systems and website are not yet up to par. A builder seeking to expand across markets needs timely, consistent information on sales, margins, construction costs, inventory, and land commitments. Without it, management cannot easily compare performance across divisions or make informed decisions about capital allocation. Gandhi previously outlined a 12-to-18-month enterprise technology implementation, along with efforts to standardize sales concessions and improve the quality of operating data. Those initiatives remain important to the company's ability to scale. View has also raised the bar in its home merchandising across markets and is developing products designed to reach beyond its traditional entry-level customer base. The objective is to preserve affordability where that remains the market opportunity while broadening View's appeal to move-up buyers and customers seeking greater design and product differentiation. The Hunt capital connection The transformation is unfolding amid difficult housing economics. Slower sales, persistent affordability pressures, and costly incentives continue to strain builder margins, while land acquisition and development require substantial capital commitments long before homes generate revenue. Hunt's ownership gives View access to a larger real estate investment organization and a longer-term investment perspective. Its recent partnership with Wafra to establish Strata Land Partners adds another potentially valuable capability. Strata launched with projects comprising approximately 1,300 single-family lots and a mandate to provide flexible land-financing solutions for public and private homebuilders and developers nationwide. items.title: Trademark And Morgan To Build Luxury Apartments In Oak Lawn: The DFW Deal Sheet
items.description: Two major commercial real estate firms began work on a luxury multifamily project that will occupy a full city block near Uptown. Courtesy of Trademark Property Co. A rendering of the multifamily community being built at 3900 Lemmon Ave. in Dallas Trademark Property Co. and Morgan Group broke ground on their 362-unit community at 3900 Lemmon Ave. in Dallas’ Oak Lawn neighborhood. items.title: Macerich In Default On Almost $400M In Mall Debt
items.description: Wikimedia Commons/Charlie Brewer Macerich has defaulted on $399M in mall loans across two properties, the company announced in its third-quarter earnings call. On Oct. 6, it defaulted on a $74M loan on the 691K SF Fashion Outlets of Niagara Falls in New York. On Nov. 2, it defaulted on a $325M loan on the 974K SF Fresno Fashion Fair mall in California. Macerich had previously announced a $76M default on Twenty Ninth Street, an open-air lifestyle center in Boulder, Colorado. Macerich executives did not offer additional details on the defaults. “I can't really talk too much about these mortgages that are in default,” Macerich CEO Jackson Hsieh said on the call. “Lenders are listening or whatever, it's not very fair. So let's just say we are in default. We're still having conversations, and we'll let you know when we got more to say, but that's what it is.” Macerich is in the midst of a multiquarter plan to rebalance its portfolio and improve its balance sheet by offloading a number of underperforming properties, with a goal of selling or giving back $300M to $400M in assets and land. The company is on track to achieve that objective this year and has sold about $290M worth of dispositions this year to date, Macerich Chief Financial Officer Daniel Swanstrom said on the call. Macerich reported a $16.7M loss in the quarter, though that was an improvement from the same period last year, when it reported an approximately $90M loss, according to filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission . The Niagara outlet mall is on the disposition list. Its loan has been modified twice already, including a three-year extension when it originally matured in 2020 and another after missing its 2023 maturity date, CoStar News reported. Its occupancy has dropped as low as 60% in recent years. The Fresno mall is not on the list of properties for sale. There, Macerich is in the middle of large-scale renovations to public spaces and is adding new tenants, including a $22M Dick's House of Sport, which is expected to open by mid-2028. The mall's special servicer is negotiating terms that would temporarily hold off enforcement of the loan default. Macerich is also still acquiring properties. On its earnings call, Hsieh teased an off-market mall purchase that is under contract now and should close by the end of the year. Malls broadly have been on a rebound. Values were up 13% over the past year, more than double the increase in all CRE prices, The Wall Street Journal reported in September . items.title: Protesters Break Into Amsterdam Microsoft Data Center Site As Opposition Swells Across Europe
items.description: Around 150 to 200 protesters were arrested in Amsterdam last Friday after breaking into the construction site of a new Microsoft data center in an attempt to halt construction. Organized by the group Geef Tegengas, with participants from the grassroots organization Extinction Rebellion and pro-Palestine groups, it was the latest in a series of protests amid widespread backlash against data centers across Europe. Smaller protests took place the same day outside of a data center near Berlin, in Warsaw by the Polish parliament, at the main square in Zagreb, Croatia, in the center of Dublin, and in Bristol in the UK. Unsplash/Winston Chen The protests follow hot on the heels of U.S. midterm elections in which voters backed anti-data-center candidates at almost every level of government . Approximately 500 protesters broke into the Amsterdam site on Friday afternoon by breaking open the fence, while hundreds more gathered outside. Some demonstrators climbed onto cranes and the roof of the construction site near Sloterdijk train station in the Westpoort district. Another demonstration, organized by Fossiel Vrij Nederland in solidarity with the other groups, took place outside of the construction site, with 300 to 400 demonstrators joining in. “All over the world, ordinary people are resisting the construction of data centers. And rightly so: data centers guzzle water and energy, cause noise pollution, and contribute to the further heating of the planet,” Martijn Dekkers, spokesperson for Extinction Rebellion, said in a statement ahead of the protest. Police responded swiftly to protesters who broke into the site, arresting between 150 and 200 demonstrators who did not leave after being ordered to do so. Local news reports indicated that police used pepper spray and, in some cases, physical force to remove protesters who repeatedly ignored police requests. A spokesperson for Geef Tegengas, which translates to "give pushback," told local news broadcaster AT5 that they were displeased with the overall police response. “There is a right to demonstrate in this country, yet that right is being disregarded; even the march toward the data center was not facilitated,” a spokesperson said. A formal complaint was filed by the owner of the property, Oaktree-backed Pure Data Centres . “We understand that this project stirs up strong emotions, and we respect people’s right to express their opinions in a peaceful manner. However, we do not condone any actions that violate the law or put people’s safety at risk,” a Microsoft spokesperson said in a statement. The Microsoft data center in question, set to be the largest in Amsterdam, has been the subject of debate over the past few months. The facility consists of three 85-meter-tall towers, a design that bypasses current regulations for “hyperscale” data centers. Plans for the data center date back to 2016, before the municipality placed a ban on new data centers in the summer of 2019 due to grid capacity and land scarcity. The facility has changed hands twice since then. The facility does not fall under the national ban, in effect since Jan. 1, 2024, against large-scale data centers with a connection capacity of 70 megawatts or more and that span more than 10 hectares outside of the Eemshaven and Wieringermeer regions. The province of Noord-Holland previously stated that the plans predate the ban, and while the facility’s 78 MW capacity is above the limit, its built floor area is under 10 hectares. The protest comes as grid operators across the Netherlands struggle with congestion. Data centers are predicted to account for approximately 15% of the country's electricity use by 2030, up from 4.6% in 2024, according to Statistics Netherlands. items.title: Servicers need to update analytics as retention rate drops
items.description: Servicers need to update analytics as retention rate drops By Colin McNamara Published November 09, 2026, 1:53 p.m. EST 3 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Expert Quote: "Traditional rate-based retention strategies aren't effective for borrowers who are motivated by access to equity" — Bob Hart, President of Mortgage Technology at ICE Supporting Data: Cash-outs accounted for 75% of all refinance-portfolio attrition in the third quarter. Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. Servicers are losing business as retention rates drop, signaling a need for more advanced analytics and a better understanding of borrowers. Refinance retention dropped four percentage points to 27% from the second to third quarter, according to the Intercontinental Exchange's latest mortgage monitor report . The retention among rate-and-term refinancers fell nine percentage points to 30%, while cash-out retention held at 26%. Servicers retained just 15% of cash-out borrowers who took out loans in 2019 or earlier. Processing Content "Get more advanced with your analytics," Andy Walden, head of mortgage and housing market research at ICE, told National Mortgage News. "Get deeper insight in terms of who's refinancing and why they're refinancing, and really incorporate that cash-out refinance scoring and propensity to refinance into your marketing effort." Andy Walden, head of mortgage and housing market research at ICE (Intercontinental Exchange) Cash-outs accounted for 75% of all refinance-portfolio attrition, which is a harder group to retain. Equity was the clear focal point for borrowers looking to refinance, and servicers who ran an in-the-money analytic off their book missed a large chunk of potential business, Walden added. "Traditional rate-based retention strategies aren't effective for borrowers who are motivated by access to equity rather than interest rate savings," said Bob Hart, president of mortgage technology at ICE, in a press release Monday. "To retain these borrowers, servicers need better visibility into their equity positions and the ability to engage them before they look elsewhere." Home equity continues to grow Borrowers collectively held a record third-quarter high $17.5 trillion in home equity, up 1.4% year over year. Tappable equity that can be accessed while maintaining a 20% cushion rose 1.2% to an average of $204,000 per borrower, a $16,600 jump from a year ago, according to the report. The number of equity millionaires also hit a third quarter record, as 2.4 million mortgage holders had at least $1 million in equity, a 6% increase from the same period last year. California accounted for 49% of the country's equity millionaires, followed by New York at 8% and New Jersey at 6%, the report found. "Home equity products, lines of credit and second liens continue to be the focal point for the market that drove the bulk of equity extraction in the first half of this year," Walden said. "Understanding borrowers and where they stand, ... whether they're a cash-out refinance or a home equity line of credit candidate, and making sure you have those pipelines set up and flowing; that's the key part from an equity standpoint." In a high-rate environment , cash-outs made up a greater share of refinances, as homeowners gave up historically low mortgage rates and took on higher monthly payments to access equity. Cash-out transactions accounted for roughly 14% of rate locks in recent weeks, while purchase loans represented 80% of rate locks, according to the report. Adjustable-rate mortgages made up more than 10% of early October rate locks as Freddie Mac's 30-year fixed-rate mortgage surged above 7%. The points-adjusted spread between 5/1 ARMs and 30-year fixed loans expanded from about 75 basis points this summer to more than 100 basis points early last month, further increasing the attractiveness of ARMs. That spread has since narrowed to about 87 basis points, the report found. items.title: Nicolas Retsinas, former Clinton housing official, dies
items.description: Nicolas Retsinas, former Clinton housing official, dies By Brad Finkelstein CloseText About Brad twitter nmnbrad mailto bradley.finkelstein@arizent.com linkedin brad-finkelstein-8b2b9a5/ Published November 09, 2026, 1:44 p.m. EST | Updated November 09, 2026, 1:51 p.m. EST 2 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Key Insight: After leaving government service, Nic Retsinas was a leader in affordable housing Expert Quote: "It was an honor for me to work with Nic." — Scott Olson Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. Nicolas Retsinas, a former Clinton administration housing official, passed away on Nov. 4 after an extended illness; he was 79 years old. Details of his passing come from golocalprov.com, a website for his hometown of Providence, Rhode Island, as well as an online obituary. Processing Content In 1987, Retsinas became head of the Rhode Island Housing and Mortgage Finance Corp., a position he occupied until 1993. Later, he would return to become its board chair from 2015 through 2020. A statement posted on LinkedIn by the organization now known as RIHousing noted Retsinas "helped our agency start a new chapter. His impact is still present today in our work as a leading housing resource for Rhode Islanders, and his legacy will live on in the organizations, communities, and people he affected." Pres. Bill Clinton named Retsinas to be his Federal Housing Commissioner in 1993; in 1996, under the Vacancy Act, Clinton appointed him interim director of the Office of Thrift Supervision. Retsinas held the FHA post until 1998, at which time he left government service to become director of the Joint Center for Housing Studies at Harvard University. In his post-government service life, he would take board positions at the Center for Responsible Lending, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp., the Federal Housing Finance Board, Freddie Mac, and the Neighborhood Reinvestment Corp., among other organizations. In addition, Retsinas was the chair of the board of directors of Habitat for Humanity International. He was inducted into the National Housing Hall of Fame. "Nic Retsinas believed that everyone deserved access to affordable, decent housing in thriving communities, and spent his professional life working to make that a reality," said Mike Calhoun, president of CRL, said in a press release. "He championed policy initiatives to address critical housing and community development needs. He also was a generous friend and mentor to many in the housing community." Retsinas' reforms while serving as FHA commissioner paved the way for the agency's critical role in preserving homeownership during the 2008 housing crisis, a statement from Scott Olson, executive director of the Community Home Lenders of America, said. "His commitment to affordable housing was evident in his enthusiasm for the cause, his record of public service, and his leadership at the Harvard Joint Center for Housing Studies," Olson said. "It was an honor for me to work with Nic. He will be sorely missed." At the Harvard Joint Center for Housing Studies, Retsinas and his wife Joan endowed the Nicolas P. and Joan B. Retsinas Faculty Directorship, to ensure it will always be led by an eminent housing practitioner or scholar, the Center said in a LinkedIn post. "We are deeply saddened to share that Nic Retsinas, who led our Center from 1998 to 2010, has passed away," the post said. "Nic was a tireless advocate for inclusive, equitable housing policy, and his vision continues to shape our work." According to an online obituary, Retsinas is survived by his wife Joan; his children Amy Romero (Andrew), Jennifer Retsinas and Gregory Retsinas (Julie); and his sister Paulette Retsinas, along with five grandchildren. items.title: Lenders face more TCPA suits despite litigation trend easing
items.description: Lenders face more TCPA suits despite litigation trend easing By Andrew Martinez CloseText About Andrew twitter andrewomartinez mailto andrew.martinez@arizent.com linkedin andrewomartinez Published November 09, 2026, 6:00 a.m. EST | Updated November 09, 2026, 6:03 a.m. EST 3 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email What's at Stake: More lenders face penalties of up to $1,500 per "willful" violation of the law for alleged mortgage solicitations. Supporting Data: Federal Telephone Consumer Protection Act lawsuits against all defendants are down on a monthly basis, but still up 13% on the year. Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. Consumers are hitting mortgage lenders with spam call lawsuits as fast as they can swat them away. Seven more origination shops have been sued for Telephone Consumer Protection Act claims since August, after dozens of lenders were sued for alleged violations this year. That litigation has poured in despite many of those earlier mortgage cases being settled or dismissed outright. Processing Content Companies can run afoul of the law if they send two or more unwanted phone calls in a 12-month period to a customer on the national Do Not Call Registry. While some of the latest lawsuits allege that lenders hit that small threshold, other consumers describe a harassment campaign of mortgage solicitations spanning months. "Consumers in the United States are united in their disdain for unsolicited marketing calls and texts," wrote attorney Max Morgan of The Weitz Firm on behalf of one of the latest plaintiffs, in a statement Friday. "Congress has warned telemarketers about the consequences of disturbing people without their permission." Penalties for each call can range from $500 to $1,500 for a willful and knowing violation. Real estate firms have paid out massive settlements in past years in TCPA cases, although a mortgage lender hasn't agreed to a large public settlement in a case this year. Who's being sued? Some of the latest real estate companies named as defendants in recent months have already been sued this year. They include: Barrett Financial Group , with $9.96 billion in volume year-to-date per Modex; eMortgage Funding , with $769 million in volume; GFS Home Loans , with $872 million in volume; Mortgage Pros , with $1.22 billion in volume; Mutual of Omaha Mortgage , with $8.2 billion in volume; Swift Home Loans , with $3.2 billion in volume. A plaintiff also sued Premier Agency Real Estate, a Southern California-based brokerage with 27 agents. Several attorneys for both plaintiffs and defendants, and company representatives, declined to comment on the pending litigation. The cases are structured similarly, although the number of combined mortgage solicitations via text messages and phone calls varies. Christopher Laccione accuses Swift of sending him at least two dozen home loan solicitations, despite his pleas that he wasn't interested. He accused the alleged Swift callers of failing to identify their affiliation. "Upon information and belief, SHL trained its representatives to be evasive because SHL knew it was violating the TCPA and various state laws and did not want to reveal its identity to minimize complaints and litigation," attorneys for Laccione, including Max Morgan, wrote. In a motion to dismiss last month, Swift argued that the plaintiff could only prove one of the phone calls came from a Swift representative, and that the consumer did not reply "stop" to text messages offering him to end outreach. An attorney and representative for the company didn't respond to requests for comment. Litigation exposure easing? In some recent motions to dismiss, lenders have begun to cite a landmark TCPA decision this summer, in which an appellate court held that the law doesn't cover text messages. None of the recent class action suits rely on sole accusations of text message outreach. Of the earlier cases filed against the industry this year, lenders have reached resolutions in at least a dozen of those filings. Tomo Mortgage and LendingTree reached undisclosed settlements in respective TCPA cases this year, while other lenders filed joint motions to dismiss with plaintiffs that did not describe settlements. The torrid pace of TCPA litigation against businesses nationwide has slowed somewhat. While federal TCPA complaints are still up around 13% on the year through October, their monthly pace has fallen, according to WebRecon . September's 191 nationwide TCPA complaints were down 27% from the same time last year. Andrew Martinez Reporter Andrew Martinez joined National Mortgage News in January 2022. items.title: Casino Mogul Steve Wynn Sells His $70 Million Central Park Condo as Manhattan Luxury Market Heats Up
items.description: Casino billionaire Steve Wynn has finally unloaded his Central Park duplex penthouse, making it the top luxury sale of a record-breaking week in Manhattan . The mogul's prewar condo at 50 Central Park South—first listed in 2022 for $90 million, the most expensive in the country at the time—eventually saw its price drop to $70 million. Even at this steep discount, it still took two years for the condo to find a taker. The duplex went into contract last week with Serena Boardman of Sotheby's International Realty as the listing agent (co-exclusive with Deborah Grubman of Corcoran). The sale means the casino magnate failed to turn a profit on the 10,875-square-foot condo. But given that, according to Forbes , Wynn is worth $4.3 billion, he likely isn't sweating it too much. The Billionaires Row duplex takes up the 30th and 31st floors within the 36-story Ritz-Carlton Residences, formerly the Hotel St. Moritz, which opened in 1930. The top 12 floors are the private homes. Loading... A luxury condo on the 30th and 31st floors at 50 Central Park South overlooking the park listed $70,000,000 was last week's top sale in Manhattan. Realtor.com The penthouse, formerly owned by real estate developer Christopher M. Jeffries , comes with an esteemed pedigree. It was Jeffries' Millennium Partners that purchased the Emory Roth –designed building in 1999 and reimagined it along with the Ritz-Carlton Hotel Co. Jeffries was once married to Princess Yasmin Aga Khan , the only child of Prince Aly Khan and movie legend Rita Hayworth . Yet the real selling point of the duplex is its sweeping Central Park views. With floors that aren't too high, from the vantage of the 45-foot long terrace, it feels as if one is sitting in the famed park's trees—a "bird's-eye perspective," as the listing puts it. Another terrace along the western wall stretches 28 feet. With three bedrooms, four full baths, and two half-baths, the prewar unit features 10 grandly arched windows, a marble staircase, 15-foot coffered ceilings, and a living room that used to be the St. Moritz ballroom. Modern touches include a chef's kitchen; a breakfast room with its own terrace; a primary bedroom with Central Park views, en suite bathroom, gym, and dressing room; a staff room with laundry; and a library. Loading... A terrace facing Central Park gives extraordinary "bird's-eye" views and likely clinched the sale. Realtor.com As the condo sits atop the flagship Ritz-Carlton hotel, it comes with access to the amenities of the global luxury name, including the La Prairie spa and health club, a business center, the Contour Bar and Lounge, in-room dining services, and housekeeping services. The unit has $31,362 in monthly dues on top of $15,500 in taxes. As for why a property offering such grandeur may have taken so long to move, luxury broker Michael Reisor with Compass-affiliated Reisor.Team, who is familiar with the building, says, "Properties like this are wonderful but specific. There's a more limited buyer pool." Despite the park views and architectural significance, it's still a century-old building, and buyers at this price range have their pick. However, "when buyers at this level want prewar charm and detail, there is only one way to get it authentically, and that is to buy of that era," he says. "Are there people in droves wanting to pay at this level for prewar? No, but there are people who do. It's usually a more sophisticated buyer. "They want that, 'This is classic New York .'" Loading... The unit has plenty of prewar charm, including arched windows and coffered 15-foot ceilings. Realtor.com The final price isn't yet known, but Reisor says, "We can assume it was right around [the ask price], if not right on." The buyer hasn't been revealed, and listing agent Boardman did not return a call for comment. One unique aspect of the 50 Central Park prewar is that it is a condo, not a co-op. Prewar buildings—built between the late 1880s and 1939—are typically co-ops. In general, condos outsell co-ops each week—and after two weeks of the gap between them being slim, for the week ending Nov. 8, condos were far ahead, 34 contracts versus 7. Co-ops tend to be cheaper, with an average ask of $8.6 million last week versus $10.5 million for condos, according to Olshan Realty . Another unusual feature of the sprawling duplex is that it has only three bedrooms. Often condos at this scale have expanded to four or more. Last week's top sale, a $31 million penthouse condo at 111 Murray St. in Tribeca, had five bedrooms. Loading... Many of the windows within the unit come with sweeping Central Park views. Realtor.com "It's more of a psychological sticking point than an actual need," Reisor says of a high-end buyer's desire for plentiful bedrooms. "They think, 'At a certain price, I should be overflowing with bedrooms.' Even if they never need them." Whoever snapped up the trophy unit likely wanted to be in that particular building, which is low-density, has only 11 private residences inside of a global luxury brand, and comes with a glamorous history and illustrious architect. "It could be someone high-profile," Reisor speculates of the mystery buyer. "Someone high-profile would want something like this." Manhattan luxury is still booming The Wynn sale was one of a slew of high-end contracts last week, with 45 signed, a big leap of 11 over the week before, and the biggest luxury sales week for the entire year. Of that, an astonishing 14 sales were priced over $10 million. The New York City pied-à-terre tax doesn't seem to be squeezing the top end of the market. Reisor says last week's surge of luxury (over $4 million) buys can be attributed to the midterm elections. "We always see a freeze-up before elections," he says. "The enemy to any financial market, including the housing market, is uncertainty. The biggest thing in play is that the election happened; it's over." items.title: David Muir Shares Rare Look at Personal Life Ahead of His Birthday—Inside His $7 Million Lakeside Estate in Upstate New York
items.description: When it comes to his personal life, famed journalist David Muir tends to keep quiet, but the “World News Tonight” anchor recently pulled back the curtain just before his 53rd birthday. In a Nov. 7 Instagram post , the ABC News anchor shared a wholesome update—a snap of his German short-haired pointer, Axel , as the pair set out to enjoy the fall foliage . Although Muir let the photo speak for itself—offering nothing more than an autumnal leaf emoji as the caption—he occasionally uploads content of Axel, usually to show off their outdoor adventures. In a 2025 interview with People magazine , the broadcaster shared some rare insight into his home life, noting that while he’s based in Manhattan for work, he enjoys retreating to a spot just outside his hometown of Syracuse . “I’d say my most comfortable element is being outside, covered in mud,” he told the publication, adding that he had recently taken a trip to his property in upstate New York , enjoying the surroundings despite the fact that it had been “pouring rain.” Loading... News anchor David Muir tends to keep his personal life private, but he recently shared a glimpse into his weekend just ahead of his 53rd birthday. Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for TIME Loading... The journalist posted a sweet photo of his dog, Axel, indicating his excitement for the fall foliage. David Muir/Instagram Loading... Muir owns a $7 million home on Skaneateles Lake, a small town near Syracuse, NY. Thomas/Adobe Stock In 2019, Muir purchased a $7 million property on Skaneateles Lake —a small town about a 30-minute drive from Syracuse. “This job takes me all over the world, and I can’t think of a better place to catch my breath,” he told Syracuse.com at the time. The 4,300-square-foot abode is a single-family home set on a 6-acre plot of land with water access. The six-bedroom, 2.5-bathroom dwelling was built in 1890 and seems to be the perfect place to escape from the bustle of the city—or a job as demanding as Muir’s. “When you’re out there on the lake, smelling the same air that you smelled when you were on your BMX bike back when you were a kid, there’s something really fueling about that and connected about it,” he told People magazine in 2025. “You just feel like you’re home again.” Over the years, Muir has invited his Instagram followers to enjoy the dazzling lake views he enjoys during his weekends away. In a 2020 post , he remarked, “I love being home,” in a caption of a photo of himself cracking a smile while enjoying a boat ride across the lake. A few distinct features of Muir’s historic home have taken up real estate on his Instagram profile, as well, including the charming wraparound porch that hugs the Skaneateles Lake property, which made an appearance in a 2022 post he shared for his sister’s birthday, where he made a note to give a shoutout to “porches.” Loading... Muir occasionally offers a glimpse of his weekend routine, which often includes boat rides with Axel. David Muir/Instagram Loading... In one post, his lakeside estate can be seen, boasting a beautiful porch. David Muir/Instagram Loading... "I love being home," Muir wrote in a 2020 post. David Muir/Instagram Loading... In 2025, Muir offloaded his beautiful brick townhouse in the West Village for $6.85 million. Google Earth Muir tends to keep his Manhattan residence under wraps for privacy, but in 2025, he bid farewell to the West Village townhouse he called home for more than 12 years. He purchased the 2,280-square-foot abode for $4.2 million in 2013, the same year he became the host of “World News Tonight,” following in Diane Sawyer ’s footsteps. Located on West Fourth Street, the three-bedroom, three-bathroom structure was built in 1877 by Alexander M. McKean , and Muir put it on the market for $7.5 million in April 2025. “Inside, the original details of this 15 foot wide house have been lovingly restored,” the listing explained . “The renovation maintains and respects the character of this remarkable home, while bringing it completely up-to-date, upgrading electricity, plumbing, and gas service but keeping and restoring original details including hardware, flooring, fixtures, and historic plaster medallions and moldings throughout.” Perhaps the most stunning feature of the townhouse was the primary bedroom, which spanned the entire fourth level of the building. With a bed area that faced over quiet gardens and a full wall of closets, the suite also included a spacious office and a windowed bathroom with a vintage claw-foot tub. The home lingered on the market for a few weeks before it was removed and relisted, but nearly six months later, it was sold for $6.85 million. items.title: Multifamily Buyer & Seller Sentiment Improves in Q1
items.description: Multifamily Buyer & Seller Sentiment Improves in Q1 April 15, 2025 3 Minute Read Underwriting assumptions for core multifamily assets improved in Q1, while those for value-add assets slightly weakened. Buyer and seller sentiment improved for both core and value-add assets. This comes despite the Federal Reserve indicating a slower pace of interest rate cuts this year as it awaits more clarity on policy shifts by the Trump administration. Figure 1: Quarter-over-Quarter Change in IRR Target & Cap Rates for Core Multifamily Assets Source: CBRE Research, Q1 2025. The average core multifamily going-in cap rate fell by 6 basis points (bps) to 4.83% in Q1, while the average exit cap rate fell by 3 bps to 5.00%. Core unlevered IRR targets decreased by 6 bps to 7.58%. Core underwriting metrics are now in line with where they were in mid-2023. The spread between going-in and exit cap rates for core assets increased to 19 bps in Q1. The spread is expected to increase over the next two years, with going-in cap rates compressing more than exit cap rates as the Fed continues to cut rates. Sixteen of the 19 markets tracked for CBRE’s quarterly Multifamily Underwriting Survey had stable IRR targets for core assets in Q1. Three markets (Los Angeles, Miami and Washington, D.C.) saw reductions in their core-asset IRR targets and for the first time in three years no markets saw an increase. Figure 2: Buyer & Seller Sentiment for Core & Value-Add Multifamily Assets Note: Estimates of sentiment are based on the expert opinion of local CBRE investment professionals. Source: CBRE Research, Q1 2025. Core-asset buyer sentiment jumped to 65% positive in Q1 from 44% positive in Q4 2024, while core-asset sellers became less negative overall with 67% neutral sentiment vs. 57% in Q4 2024. Value-add buyers exhibited only slightly improved positive-to-neutral sentiment, while value-add sellers shifted to a higher concentration of neutral sentiment. Improving sentiment was seen primarily in the Sun Belt across product types, as well as in San Francisco for core assets only. Figure 3: Buyer Valuation Underwriting Assumptions for Core & Value-Add Multifamily Assets Source: CBRE Research, Q1 2025. Underwriting assumptions of annual asking rent growth for core and value-add assets over the next three years held steady at 2.7% and 3.1%, respectively. This stability coincides with the current recovery in rent growth following a generational wave of new supply in many of our tracked markets. While core assets saw improved underwriting metrics, value-add going-in cap rates increased by 7 bps to 5.32% and exit cap rates increased by 3 bps to 5.42%. Unlike with core assets, whose spread between going-in and exit cap rates widened in Q1, the spread for value-add assets (10 bps) declined for the second consecutive quarter. Unlevered IRR targets for value-add assets increased by 2 bps to 9.81%. Figure 4: Underwriting Assumptions for Core & Value-Add Multifamily Assets by Market, Q1 2025 *Unreported Note: Estimates are based on the expert opinion of local CBRE investment professionals. Source: CBRE Research, Q1 2025. Seven markets saw going-in cap rate compression for core assets (Atlanta, Chicago, Houston, Los Angeles, Nashville, San Francisco and Washington, D.C.), while Indianapolis saw a slight increase. No markets saw movements of more than 25 bps in either direction. For value-add assets, two markets (Austin and Miami) had lower going-in cap rates in Q1 than in Q4, while four had higher rates. While overall value-add underwriting metrics weakened slightly, buyer and seller sentiment across both core and value-add assets improved in Q1. This comes even as the market continues to seek clarity on the implications of the Trump administration’s policy changes. Throughout the rest of this year, we expect tailwinds in the multifamily sector as investors look to capitalize on improved market fundamentals, particularly in the core segment. items.title: Cushman & Wakefield Brokers $44 Million Sale of 240-Unit Apartment Community in Sheboygan, Wisconsin to Axiom Properties
items.description: Cushman & Wakefield Brokers $44 Million Sale of 240-Unit Apartment Community in Sheboygan, Wisconsin to Axiom Properties Jeremy Barewin • 11/9/2026 The Corridor garnered significant investor interest, attracting more than 25 offers The Corridor SHEBOYGAN, WISC. -- Cushman & Wakefield (NYSE: CWK), a leading global real estate services firm, today announced that its Multifamily Advisory Group has brokered the $44 million sale of The Corridor, a 240-unit Class A multifamily community in Sheboygan, Wisconsin, to Axiom Properties. Cushman & Wakefield's Brad Smith, Jack Maloney and Ralph Depasquale represented the seller, Chicago-based Midloch Investment Partners. Located at 1436 Green Street, the community was approximately 97% occupied at the time of sale. Under the seller's ownership, occupancy increased by nearly 25 percentage points in roughly 13 months. The sale also includes an in-place tax increment financing (TIF) agreement, which reimburses 65% of the incremental property tax through 2038 and enhances cash flow for the new owner. The Corridor benefits from a location within 30 minutes of more than 60,000 jobs, including major regional employers such as Kohler, Aurora Health Care, Sargento and Rockline Industries. Within a five-mile radius of the property, apartment occupancy exceeds 97%, while the area has seen no new multifamily deliveries since 2024 despite a sizeable population of renter households earning $50,000 or more annually. "Tertiary Midwest markets supported by strong employment fundamentals and limited new supply are attracting significant investor interest," said Smith, Managing Director, Cushman & Wakefield. "We received 25 offers from institutional, national, regional and private buyers, underscoring the depth of demand for stable, insulated markets like Sheboygan. As one of the largest multifamily transactions in the market in recent years, The Corridor presented a rare opportunity to acquire a high-quality asset with both strong in-place performance, cash flow stability and future upside." Completed in 2021 on a 13.44-acre site, The Corridor features one-, two- and three-bedroom residences across three residential buildings, along with a fitness center, resident lounge, community room, dog park, playground, outdoor gathering spaces and parking. items.description: 2.4 Million Mortgage Holders Are Equity Millionaires as Q3 Home Equity Hits Record High Servicer retention declined in Q3, with cash-out refinances accounting for 75% of refinance portfolio attrition. Nov. 9, 2026 Share ATLANTA & NEW YORK -- (Nov. 9, 2026) – Intercontinental Exchange, Inc. (NYSE: ICE), one of the world’s leading providers of financial market technology and data powering global capital markets, today released the November 2026 ICE Mortgage Monitor Report. The analysis finds that home equity and the number of equity millionaires both reached record third-quarter highs, creating opportunities for lenders and servicers to engage borrowers seeking access to that wealth. "Homeowners are sitting on substantial housing wealth, with 2.4 million mortgage holders now holding at least $1 million in equity,” said Andy Walden, Head of Mortgage and Housing Market Research at ICE. “In a higher rate environment, cash-outs are making up a greater share of refinances, with those homeowners giving up historically low mortgage rates and taking on higher monthly payments to tap into their equity." Key findings from the November ICE Mortgage Monitor include: Home equity reached a record third-quarter high: Mortgage holders collectively held $17.5 trillion in equity in Q3, up 1.4% year over year. Tappable equity that can be accessed while maintaining a 20% cushion rose 1.2% to an average of $204,000 per borrower, an increase of $16,600 from a year ago. The number of equity millionaires reached a Q3 record: 2.4 million mortgage holders had at least $1 million in equity, up 6% year over year, while nearly 9 million held $500,000 or more, up 4%. California accounted for 49% of the nation’s equity millionaires, followed by New York (189,000), New Jersey (141,000) and Florida (104,000). Rising rates drove increased share of cash-out refinances: Cash-out transactions accounted for 1 in 7 rate locks in recent weeks, and purchase loans accounted for roughly 80% of rate locks. ARMs remained popular due to higher rates and more attractive spreads: Adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs) accounted for more than 10% of early October rate locks as 30-year fixed rates moved above 7%. The points-adjusted spread between 5/1 ARMs and 30-year fixed loans widened from roughly 75 basis points over the summer to more than 100 basis points in early October, further increasing the attractiveness of ARMs. Refinance retention declined as cash-out activity grew: Servicers retained 27% of refinancing borrowers, down four percentage points from the prior quarter, while retention among rate-and-term refinancers fell nine percentage points to 30%. Cash-out retention held at 26%, with servicers retaining just 15% of cash-out borrowers who took out loans in 2019 or earlier. Cash-out refinances accounted for 75% of all refinance-portfolio attrition. "Traditional rate-based retention strategies aren’t effective for borrowers who are motivated by access to equity rather than interest rate savings,” said Bob Hart, President of Mortgage Technology at ICE. “To retain these borrowers, servicers need better visibility into their equity positions and the ability to engage them before they look elsewhere. By combining ICE’s retention analytics with connected technologies like MSP, Servicing Digital and Encompass, we’re helping lenders and servicers identify opportunities, connect borrowers with financing options and keep those relationships intact." Further detail on ARM, home equity, home price, and mortgage performance trends — including charts — can be found in the full ICE Mortgage Monitor report at https://mortgagetech.ice.com/resources/data-reports . About Mortgage Monitor ICE manages the nation’s leading repository of loan-level residential mortgage data and performance information covering the majority of the overall market, including tens of millions of loans across the spectrum of credit products and more than 160 million historical records. The combined insight of the ICE Home Price Index and ICE Valuation Analytics’ home price and real estate data provides one of the most complete, accurate and timely measures of home prices available, covering 95% of U.S. residential properties down to the ZIP-code level. In addition, the company maintains one of the most robust public property records databases available, covering 99.9% of the U.S. population and households from more than 3,100 counties.
